## Simple explanation

A support vector machine (SVM) separates classes by finding a boundary
that leaves as much space as possible between the boundary and nearby
training examples. Those closest examples are the support vectors.

## Technical explanation

A linear SVM optimizes a margin-based objective, commonly with hinge loss
and regularization. Kernel methods implicitly map inputs into a feature
space where nonlinear boundaries can be learned. The regularization
parameter and kernel settings affect the margin and training errors.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

SVMs can perform well on small or medium-sized datasets, especially with
high-dimensional features. Kernelized models can become costly as dataset
size grows, and probability estimates require additional calibration.

## How it works

The model chooses a separating hyperplane that balances margin size and
classification errors. Only support vectors directly determine the
boundary in the standard formulation. For nonlinear separation, a kernel
computes similarities without explicitly constructing transformed
features.

## Practical example

A text classifier can use TF-IDF features with a linear SVM to categorize
documents. Tune hyperparameters on validation data and evaluate per-class
precision and recall on a held-out test set.

## Common misconceptions

- An SVM does not necessarily produce calibrated class probabilities.
- The widest margin is defined relative to the chosen features, kernel,
  and regularization, not an absolute notion of best separation.
